Objeto indireto + objeto direto: a ordem: Indirect object + direct object: pronoun order
PASSO 1: uma frase pode ter os dois comp: STEP 1: a sentence can have both complements: «Doy el libro a Ana». The book is the direct object (what?) and Ana is the indirect object (to whom?). If you swap both for pronouns, the sentence becomes «Se lo doy». STEP 2: there's just one rule: the person pronoun (the indirect one) comes first, then the thing pronoun (the direct one). In other words, «me, te, nos, os» come before «lo, la, los, las». STEP 3: «¿Me das el libro? — Sí, te lo doy». Here «te» is the person I'm giving it to (you) and «lo» is «el libro». STEP 4: nothing goes between the two pronouns, and they never flip order: «me lo», never «lo me». STEP 5: «lo, la, los, las» agree with the thing, not the person. A feminine plural thing is always «las», whoever the person is: «Me las das», «Te las doy». STEP 6: the position is the usual one, before the conjugated verb: «Me lo dices», «No te lo digo», «Nos las trae». STEP 7: in the compound tenses, both pronouns go before «haber»: «Te lo he dicho». In the indefinido: «Me lo dio», «Te la mandé». STEP 8: English doesn't have a contracted double-pronoun form either, but it solves the same two-pronoun problem differently: when both the person and the thing are pronouns, English usually needs "to" — "I'll give it to you" — rather than stacking two bare pronouns the way Spanish does.
o português tem as contrações «mo, to, l: Some English speakers do say "give me it" or "give it me" in certain dialects, but it's regional and never the safe default; the standard form keeps the preposition. Spanish's «me lo», «te la» pattern — person-pronoun immediately before thing-pronoun, with no preposition at all — has no everyday English equivalent, so it takes real practice before it feels automatic. This combination, used constantly in everyday Spanish, is one of the biggest new habits at this level.

Se lo: quando o indireto é «le» ou «les»: Se lo: when the indirect object is «le» or «les»
PASSO 1: se o objeto indireto é de terce: STEP 1: if the indirect object is third-person («le, les») and the direct one is «lo, la, los, las», a sound clash comes up: «le lo», «les la». Spanish avoids this by swapping «le» and «les» for «se». STEP 2: «Le doy el libro a Ana» becomes «Se lo doy». «Les mando las entradas a mis padres» becomes «Se las mando». STEP 3: this «se» is not the reflexive «se». It's «le» or «les» transformed, so it doesn't say whether the person is one or several, or male or female — the listener works that out from context. STEP 4: «lo, la, los, las» agree with the thing: «Les di las llaves» becomes «Se las di», and «las» is for «llaves», not for whoever received them. STEP 5: to clarify who, add «a + person» at the end: «Se lo di a Ana», «Se las mandé a mis padres», «Se lo dije a usted». STEP 6: with the infinitive, both pronouns attach to the end: «dar + se + lo» becomes «dárselo». Since the word grows longer, you must write the accent on the original stressed syllable: «dárselo, decírtelo, mostrárselo, comprármelo, escribírselo». STEP 7: as in other cases, there are two positions: «Voy a dárselo» or «Se lo voy a dar». STEP 8: in Latin America, «os» doesn't exist: instead of «os lo digo», you say «se lo digo» for «ustedes». STEP 9: a false friend in this part: «dirección» means address (and also direction): «¿Me das tu dirección?». Email is «correo» or «correo electrónico».
a regra do «se lo» não tem equivalente n: English has nothing like the «se» substitution either, because English never runs into the same clash in the first place — it keeps the preposition, so «I gave it to him» never risks stacking two colliding third-person pronouns. Treat Spanish «se lo», «se la» as a dedicated rule to memorize rather than a translation of anything already in your English habits, and don't confuse this «se» with the reflexive «se» of «se lava» or the impersonal «se» of «se habla español» — they look identical but do something completely different.

Reflexivo + objeto direto e vocabulário: Reflexive + direct object, and vocabulary from Spain and Latin America
PASSO 1: os verbos reflexivos da aula 14: STEP 1: the reflexive verbs from lesson 14 can also take a direct object: «Me pongo la chaqueta», «Me lavo las manos». When the direct object becomes a pronoun, the reflexive comes first: «Me la pongo», «Me las lavo». STEP 2: with the third person, the reflexive «se» comes before «lo»: «Se puso el abrigo» becomes «Se lo puso». STEP 3: asking for something with two pronouns feels natural: «¿Me lo puedes explicar?», «¿Puedes explicármelo?». STEP 4: vocabulary differs between Spain and Latin America. «Móvil», «ordenador», «coche», and «billete» (Spain) correspond to «celular», «computadora», «carro», and «boleto» or «pasaje» (many Latin American countries). Both are understood everywhere; hearing the other one shouldn't come as a surprise. STEP 5: use the variant from your target region and stay consistent. In this course, the audio is from Spain, and the Latin American words are given as a note.
em português, o reflexivo e o objeto dir: English also lets a reflexive and a direct object show up together ("he put on his coat" → "he put it on"), and the pronoun order mirrors Spanish's: the thing-pronoun slots in where the noun was. What's new isn't the order so much as the habit — Spanish keeps doing this constantly in everyday speech («se lo puso»), where English just as often skips the pronoun and repeats the noun or rephrases instead.
